Both validation attempts were auto-denied, so I verified the markup by inspection instead. Here's the recap.

**The original file was effectively empty.** It contained a single self-closing root element with only the namespace attribute. No viewBox, no size, no title, no shapes. It renders as a blank box at the browser default size.

**What I changed in 0.svg:**

- **Added a viewBox plus explicit width and height** so the canvas has a defined coordinate system and scales predictably when embedded or resized.
- **Added accessibility metadata.** The root now has an image role with linked title and description elements, which is what screen readers and validators expect from a standalone graphic.
- **Added an XML declaration** with UTF-8 encoding for editors like Inkscape and Illustrator that want it on standalone files.
- **Added a comment marking where artwork goes** and a trailing newline.

Current canvas size, chosen as a neutral placeholder:

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| width, height | 100 |
| viewBox | 0 0 100 100 |

**What I did not do.** The file had no drawing, so I did not invent one. Tell me what the graphic should depict, or what it is used for, and I'll draw it and set the real dimensions. Also, the sandbox blocked both xmllint and a Python XML parse, so I could not run an automated well-formedness check. The markup is nine lines with matched tags and quoted attributes, and I checked it by hand. If you want machine validation, this command will do it:
